comments.author: Jason Bowman
comments.text:
★ SHARPENED BY MEASUREMENT — MY EARLIER FRAMING OF THIS BEAD WAS WRONG IN A WAY THAT MATTERS, AND IT PROPAGATED.

I recorded (and repeated on den-hoag-4kh.13 and den-hoag-4kh.45) that message-text assertions are IMPOSSIBLE because mkCi's asserter has no error channel and `builtins.tryEval` yields only a bool. ★ THAT REASON IS REFUTED.
MEASURED: nix-unit NATIVELY SUPPORTS `expectedError = { type = "ThrownError"; msg = "…"; }` AND IT WORKS ON `nix-unit --flake ./ci#tests` —
  probe with a matching msg → EXIT 0, 1923/1923, the probe test GREEN;
  NEGATIVE CONTROL with the msg changed to TOTALLY-DIFFERENT-MESSAGE → EXIT 1, 1922/1923, probe RED.
So the channel is real, it discriminates, and it is not silently ignored. `tryEval` is irrelevant — nix-unit does not use it for this.

★ THE OPERATIVE BLOCKER IS THE OTHER RUNNER, WHICH IS EXACTLY WHAT THIS BEAD IS ABOUT. gen's homegrown asserter (~/Documents/repos/sini/gen/ci/flakeModule.nix:20-28) evaluates `t.expr == t.expected` UNCONDITIONALLY, so an expectedError test CRASHES THE BATCH GATE rather than failing it:
  `nix eval .#checks.x86_64-linux.default.drvPath` WITH the probe → EXIT 1, `error: PROBE-MESSAGE-XYZ`
  same, probe removed → EXIT 0 (positive control).
⇒ A message-text test CAN be written and CAN pass on the nix-unit path; it simply cannot coexist with `checks.default`. That is a much narrower and more fixable statement than 'no message channel exists'.

★ AND IT NAMES THE REAL FIX: teach `assertTests` TO SKIP tests carrying `expectedError` rather than evaluating them. title: Instrument-trap case log — evidence archive for the verification-predicate laws
description:
INSTRUMENT-TRAP CASE LOG — the evidence behind the laws in memory `feedback_verification_predicate_blindness`.

WHY THIS BEAD EXISTS. The memory had grown to 238 LINES — ~25 earned traps with their full case studies. At
that size it is never recalled, and on 2026-07-28 that cost a live hit: a reviewer's strip-list search used
`grep 'removeAttrs' | grep '__coords…'` and got ZERO for lists that exist, because the key names sit on
CONTINUATION LINES.
★ THAT EXACT TRAP WAS ALREADY ENTRY 3 OF THE MEMORY, IN THOSE WORDS: "every strip site is a multi-line list
literal, so the key names and removeAttrs are never on the same line. grep | grep is line-oriented."
The memory knew. Nobody read it, because it was too big to read. That is the whole argument for the split:
LAWS stay in memory, short enough to load every session; CASES live here, queryable when a law needs its
evidence. Nothing below is deleted — this is the archive, not a summary.

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
A verification predicate (grep, census, settling test) is only evidence if its
string actually appears on the path it claims to check. Three occurrences in the
den-hoag topology arc, same shape each time — a plausible predicate returning a
clean result it structurally could not have found:

1. **Blast-radius guard** greped `containTo`, but compat *lowers* `resolve.to
   <registry-backed root kind>` into a `containTo` member, so 9 files carrying
   only `resolve.to` were invisible. Would have classified a legitimate delta as
   a bug in the rung.
2. **D6's settling test** greped `mkInstanceRegistry` to enumerate mkDen-direct
   fixtures — but den-hoag builds the registry internally, so such a fixture
   never writes that string. The grep returned empty whether or not dependents
   existed, and the plan read that emptiness as authorization to delete a live
   mechanism.
3. **Strip-site completeness grep** was `grep -rn '__entry\|…' lib/ | grep -i
   'removeAttrs\|strip'` — every strip site is a multi-line list literal, so the
   key names and `removeAttrs` are never on the same line. `grep | grep` is
   line-oriented; it returned one line, a comment.

**How to apply:** before trusting a verification predicate, ask *what does the
at-risk path actually look like in source* — then confirm the predicate matches
a known-positive instance. If it can't find one you already know exists, the
predicate is broken, not the code. Prefer the literal that survives lowering
(the key name, the constructor) over the conceptual name. An **absence** result
deserves more scrutiny than a hit: a hit is self-evidencing, an empty result is
indistinguishable from a blind predicate.

A fifth instance came from a *sweep written to criticise a hand list*: `"${x}:${y}"`
with `[^}]*` cannot span a nested interpolation, so it missed three id-construction
sites — including one (`fleet.nix:95` `cid`) sitting in plain view, which is the
known-positive that would have exposed it immediately. Working predicate for Nix
id sites: `grep -rn ':\${' lib/ --include='*.nix'`.

## The same disease in tests: a check that a degenerate result satisfies

**When an assertion quantifies over a computed set, pin the set's contents too —
otherwise a regression that empties the set passes.** `builtins.all f xs` is
vacuously true at `xs == [ ]`, so "every pair names a real node" was satisfiable
by emitting no pairs at all. Fix: assert the literal expected ids beside the
invariant.

Its twin, from the same arc: an M7 abort fixture went green because a *different*
guard (B2 stratum coherence) aborted first — the intended guard was never reached.
Caught only by a control asking **"does this test depend on the RIGHT thing"**
(point it at a single-attachment target and require red), not the weaker
**"does it depend on anything"** (remove a declaration and require red), which
passed either way.

**How to apply:** for any new guard or invariant, prove it can fail *for its own
reason* before trusting a pass. Unreachability claims need this too — an
unreachable-path abort is untestable, so prefer recording *"unreachable in this
shape, measured"* with the counter-shape named over adding a guard you cannot arm.
Three unreachability claims were asserted and disproved in one arc.

## The general form: instruments, not just predicates

**A NEGATIVE RESULT REQUIRES A POSITIVE CONTROL ON THE SAME INSTRUMENT, IN THE SAME
RUN.** Not "a known-positive somewhere" — the *same* instrument, the *same*
execution. Without one, *"it didn't fire"* and *"it cannot fire"* are the same
observation. A grep that cannot match its target and a probe that cannot fire are
one failure in two costumes.

Twice in one investigation (den-hoag `ljr`), each a step from being read as a
finding:

1. **Silence.** Two conditional throws both stayed quiet. Worth nothing alone. An
   **unconditional marker** at the same site, firing on *both* sides, is what
   converted two silences into "both links intact".
2. **The wrong observable.** A *collision* trace proves a merge descended but
   cannot separate "instrument never fires" from "code never does it".
   Re-instrumenting the *recursion branch* **tagged by depth** — family level as
   the known-positive that MUST fire (8×/15×), member level as the violation
   (0×→1×) — made the base zero a real negative.

**Corollary — apply it to the FIX, not just the diagnosis.** The first
`familyMerge` guard put its check inside the value lambda and never fired under
`attrNames`: the guard reintroduced the exact silent-until-used shape it existed to
remove. Review missed it; *arming* it caught it. So an assertion that a new guard
fires for its own reason is mandatory, never a precaution.

**And when a guard replaces an assumed invariant, the prose must change with it.**
A comment claiming uniqueness "by construction" beside code that now aborts because
it does not is this same defect in documentation form. A documented invariant that
nothing enforces is a comment, not a guarantee.

## A control must be forced to the SAME DEPTH as the subject

**Two false cleans in one probe, either of which would have certified a dead
option as safe:**

1. **Laziness hides the check.** A control setting a nonexistent option returned
   its value with no abort — the unmatched-option check was on, but the option's
   type was a **submodule**, and a submodule's check cannot fire until the
   submodule is forced. Nothing forced it. Caught only by a *second* control at a
   **different level** (top-level rather than nested), which did abort.
2. **The harness reshaped the value.** The test driver did
   `intersectAttrs expected config.expr`; passing `expected = { }` made the
   intersection empty, forcing `expr` to WHNF and never reaching a leaf. The
   subject read clean because nothing was evaluated.

⇒ **When a harness transforms the value under test, the harness is part of the
instrument and needs calibrating too.** Ask what depth your control actually
forced, not merely whether it fired.

## The fixture form: it cannot disagree with the code it was written against

Reached **three times independently in one day**, from different directions:

1. **It asserts its own premise.** A fixture hand-stamped the `id_hash` it then
   checked the reflection against. Two wrong halves validated each other and read
   as green — and they could not be fixed one at a time, because either ordering
   leaves a red intermediate.
2. **It fails in its own construction.** A shallow `//` replaced an option set
   outright, so the "arm loss" observed was the fixture's bug, reported as a
   finding about the subject.
3. **It is sampled from the agreeing case.** An invariant test asserting
   twin == stamp used the one type name *both* engines spell identically. It
   stayed green through the entire divergence it existed to catch.

⇒ When a test builds the shape under test, ask what input would make its two
sides disagree — and whether the fixture can even express it.

## Papering over the TEST, not the requirement

**An acceptance criterion that is already satisfied gives the requirement no
falsifier.** Nothing observable then distinguishes implemented-correctly,
implemented-wrongly, and not-implemented — rule 1's failure mode applied to
acceptance rather than to a probe. Watch for it when a criterion is *proposed as
a concession* ("accept that X is excluded by the existing gate"). Ask: does this
criterion hold **today**? If yes, it tests nothing.

Related traps, each earned:
- **A cited finding is still a claim until its mechanism is traced.** A finding
  that arrives with a `file:line` gets adopted verbatim; a reviewer's own error
  propagated one full revision this way.
- **A comment stating a constraint is evidence** — contradicting one needs a
  measurement, not a recollection. **But a comment describing an ABSENCE is not a
  law.** *"X never happens by Y"* may be true only because Y does not exist yet,
  and will read as a prohibition on exactly the feature that adds it. Test:
  *does this describe what the code guarantees, or what it merely does not do yet?*
- **An armed conjunction needs one perturbation per conjunct**, each moving only
  its own — one dead conjunct hides inside a `true`.

Related: agents' **absence claims** need the same scrutiny — two in this arc were
false (den v1 reported "not on this machine" when it sits at
`~/Documents/repos/denful/den`; `deriveGroup` reported missing when the dir is
`gen-derive`, not `gen-dispatch`). Positive findings held up; absence claims did
not. See [[feedback_scout_vs_ultracode_audit]].

## The predicate was SOUND but proved a DIFFERENT PROPOSITION

The sharpest instance yet, because nothing about the run looks wrong. `grep '2\.3'
<paper> → 0`, with the positive control firing, establishes **the paper has no
§2.3**. It was reported as **"our §2.3 citation came from a restatement"** — a
claim about the provenance of *our* section number, which nothing in the run
touched. The tree was never searched for what `§2.3` refers to; it turned out to
be the project's *own* spec section, used correctly at ~69 sites.

⇒ A positive control proves the instrument works. **It does not prove you measured
the proposition you reported.** After any clean run, restate the conclusion and ask
which command bears on *that sentence*. Both this and the orchestrator's own errors
below were caught only by someone re-running a claim instead of accepting it.

## Six more shapes, all from one session, most of them mine

1. **A filter that excludes the at-risk tree.** `grep -rE 'pat' repo/ --include='*.nix' specs/`
   — the `--include` applies to *every* path, so every `.md` spec was silently
   skipped. Two sweeps vacuous. **Never combine `--include=` with a multi-tree search;**
   run each tree separately.
2. **The literal differs by a hyphen.** Searched `local stratification` and `locally
   stratified`; the file said `local-stratification`. Use `[-_ ]?` between words in
   any multi-word predicate.
3. **A removal check that greps the phrasing you wrote.** A figure was reported
   removed; the verification was `grep '~50 seconds'` → 0. The claim had only been
   *reworded* — the tilde went, `50 seconds` stayed. **When removing a claim, grep
   for the NUMBER and the CONCEPT, never the sentence you happened to write.**
4. **Checking the parent for a repo.** `git rev-parse` at `~/Documents/papers` →
   "not a repository", so the tree was declared unversioned. The repo was one level
   down at `papers/den-architecture`. Git stops at the filesystem boundary; a
   negative at the parent says nothing about children.
5. **The wrong vocabulary entirely.** A sweep for the token `enrich` over a corpus
   returned 0 — but the surface spells enrichment `resolve { <non-schema-key> = … }`.
   The concept had no lexical form matching the search.
6. **Forcing only the spine.** `builtins.length` / `attrNames` force a list spine or
   key set, never the values. A relaxation matrix reported OK across every arm and
   *could not have caught the throw*; a cost probe returned a flat ~0.01s across all
   n. Fix: `builtins.deepSeq` **plus a sentinel that aborts**, proving the force
   reached the values before any number is reported.

## The TOOL itself can return a false zero — cross-check with a second one

One agent reported `grep -rnE` through a harness wrapper returning **0 hits** in a file where a direct grep
returned 28; it cross-checked with `ripgrep` rather than trusting the zero. **That specific fault did NOT
reproduce** — a second agent got identical counts from `grep -rnE`, per-file `grep -nE`, and `rg -n`, and
found the likelier cause of its own earlier zero was a *relative* path with the working directory resetting
between calls. So treat the wrapper-fault claim as unestablished; I over-generalised one report into a
session-wide instrument fault and propagated it to three agents before it was checked.

**The discipline survives the retraction, on its own merits.** A relative path that silently resolves
elsewhere produces exactly the same false zero as a broken tool, and *that* is common. Cross-checking is also
what closed a real completeness question in the same arc: a sweep for ordering guards under **non-local
spellings**, with a positive control that fired on the one row the primary predicate structurally could not
see, converted "the table is asserted complete" into "the table is measured complete".

⇒ **A negative from a recursive/wrapped search deserves a second instrument before it is reported.** The
positive-control rule catches a predicate that cannot match; it does **not** catch a tool that does not
traverse. Confirm an absence with a different tool (`rg` vs `grep`) or a direct per-file read, and prefer
per-file over recursive whenever the answer is load-bearing.

**Same class: a tool that silently omits the field you queried.** `bd show --json` returns no `comments`
key at all — only `comment_count`. Querying it for comment content yields nothing, indistinguishable from
"there are no comments", and would make an absence claim about a tracker comment *unfalsifiable from the
JSON alone*. The agent that settled it went to the raw store (`.beads/beads.jsonl`) instead of trusting
either the renderer or the JSON. **When an absence claim rests on a tool's output, check that the tool
actually carries the field** — and go to the storage layer when the answer matters.

## Timing: work-dominated reproduces, floor-dominated does not

A wall-clock figure was called an "internal impossibility" because a traversal
appeared to cost less than importing the library it runs in — comparing *my* import
floor against *their* traversal number. Three machines measured three different
import floors (0.011 / 0.020 / 0.175 s) because the flake resolves a dependency via
`fetchTree` and the cost depends on local store state.

⇒ **Work-dominated figures reproduce cross-machine; floor-dominated ones do not.**
Evidence: the same exponential arm came in at 12.417 s and 12.473 s on two machines
while the floors disagreed by 16×. Quote a floor-dominated number only labelled
environment-specific and never load-bearing; rest the claim on the **shape**.
notes:
★ CASE ADDED 2026-07-28 -- A RECORDED MEASUREMENT WHOSE STATED PREDICATE COULD
NOT HAVE PRODUCED ITS NUMBERS. This one is ours, in the tracker, and it survived
because its CONCLUSION was right.

SITE: den-hoag-9xo.54's verdict comment, 2026-07-28 19:12.

TWO DEFECTS, found by an independent re-run that reproduced the comment's
241/31/0/9 firing counts and its membership rows exactly:

(1) WRONG PIN CITED. The comment names arm A as "den v1 4911b7f2 (the corpus's
    own lock)". At nix-config HEAD the lock is 99cc0c5a. 4911b7f2 is the lock of
    the PARITY-PIN corpus b0b20769 (parity/flake.nix:12) -- a DIFFERENT corpus.
    The two are not interchangeable: at the parity pin arm (b) fails EARLIER and
    differently than at HEAD, so a claim carrying the wrong pin is not merely
    imprecise, it points at a tree with different behaviour.

(2) ★★ THE PREDICATE COULD NOT HAVE RUN. The comment reports membership measured
    "at BOTH the pin and nix-config HEAD" via `home-manager.users` and
    `config.users.users`. At den-hoag c42df53 -- code-identical to the 222af84 the
    comment cites, the diff being .beads/beads.jsonl ONLY -- BOTH predicates FAIL
    under --override-input den, at BOTH revisions, including with the runbook's
    nested override set: `attribute 'id_hash' missing`, collections.nix:205, all
    seven hosts (den-hoag-9xo.61). Whatever route produced that comment's arm-B
    membership, IT WAS NOT A MATERIALIZED-CONFIG READ ON THIS CONFIGURATION.

★ WHY THIS CASE IS WORTH MORE THAN THE USUAL ONE: THE CONCLUSION WAS CORRECT. The
independent run reaches the same verdict the comment reached. So nothing
downstream broke, no bad decision was made, and there was no symptom to notice --
which is exactly why a mis-stated predicate can sit in the record indefinitely.
A wrong answer gets caught by its consequences; A RIGHT ANSWER OBTAINED BY AN
UNSTATED ROUTE IS CAUGHT BY NOTHING. It is only detectable by someone re-running
the stated recipe, which is why the recipe must be stated well enough to re-run
and why a report must say what it ACTUALLY executed rather than what it intended
to execute.

⇒ THE LAW THIS SHARPENS: a report's METHOD line is a load-bearing claim and gets
the same scrutiny as its result. When a result is reported, the stated instrument
must be the instrument that ran -- and where an agent fell back to a different
route (a scratch probe, a graph-level read, a proxy attribute), the FALLBACK is
the finding, because it usually means the intended path is BLOCKED. Here the
fallback would have surfaced den-hoag-9xo.61, the P0 materialization ladder,
several hours earlier than it did.

COUNTER-EXAMPLE IN THE SAME ARC, showing the discipline working: the re-run that
found this stated its own fallback explicitly -- a scratch-only `__probeBindings`
appended to crossVia's return reading the corpus's own `resolved-users` quirk
collection -- AND stated the limitation that follows (a graph-level read, not
cross-checkable against arm (b)'s materialized users.users, since that is the
blocked path). Same substitution, declared instead of silent.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
★ CASE ADDED 2026-07-28 -- THE DEAD CONTROL. Caught by the agent itself, one
step before it shipped a result resting on it. This is the arc's recurring shape
in its purest form, and it is worth more than the finding it nearly corrupted.

THE SETUP. Measuring whether den.schema.<K>.isolated cuts the constraint ancestor
walk. A verdict of "isolation does not cut the walk" is an ABSENCE claim, so it
needs a TOOK-EFFECT control: proof that `isolated` did something ELSE in the same
run, or the null result is indistinguishable from a declaration that never
registered.

THE DEAD CONTROL. First attempt: u0 = host package reaches flake.packages, no
isolation. u1 = same, isolated. Result: u0 = [ ], u1 = [ ].
Read naively -- "u1 is empty, so isolation fired" -- this CONFIRMS the control.
★ BOTH ARMS WERE EMPTY BECAUSE THE BASELINE NEVER WORKED. mkOutputPolicy
(den modules/policies/flake.nix) is gated on `has-flake-output`, which reads the
INNER eval's options.flake; the trimmed probe template lacked
inputs.den.flakeOutputs.packages, so the gate was FALSE and NO package ever
reached the flake -- isolated or not.

THE FIX AND WHAT IT COST. Adding that import inside the denTest module turned the
baseline green (v0 = ["one"]), giving a control that can actually discriminate:
v1 (no isolation) = ["one"], v2 (isolated) = [ ]. Only THEN does the measurement
arm mean anything.

★ THE LAW, in the agent's own words: "A PREDICATE THAT RETURNS 'EMPTY' FOR THE
REASON YOU WANT AND FOR A REASON YOU DID NOT NOTICE IS INDISTINGUISHABLE UNTIL
YOU RUN THE POSITIVE ARM."

WHY IT GENERALISES BEYOND THIS ARC: the control was DESIGNED CORRECTLY -- the
agent knew an absence claim needs a took-effect arm and built one. The failure was
that THE CONTROL ITSELF NEEDED A CONTROL. Its "off" state and its "broken" state
produce the same observation, so it can only be trusted once its ON state has been
seen to differ. ⇒ A CONTROL IS NOT VALIDATED BY BEING RUN; IT IS VALIDATED BY
BEING SEEN TO MOVE. Every took-effect arm therefore needs its own baseline showing
the observable is ALIVE before the perturbation -- three arms, not two.

COMPARE the same session's membership work, which got this right by construction:
its perturbation control moved blade from [shuo,sini,will] to
[dvicory,pol,shuo,sini,theutz,vic,will] WHILE cortex, untouched, HELD. A control
that moves one thing and holds another cannot be dead in the way this one was.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
★ CASE ADDED 2026-07-28 -- THE PREDICATE RAN AT THE WRONG POINT IN THE PIPELINE.
Built, reported 0, discarded by its own author before it reached a verdict. The
sharpest instance yet, because the predicate was WELL-FORMED and the DATA IT NEEDED
DID NOT EXIST YET AT THE PLACE IT LOOKED.

THE TASK: does any identity key cover more than one distinct content?

THE BLIND VERSION. The check ran AT THE STAMP SITES (compile.nix:426/:436),
signing content by `name + attrNames`. IT REPORTED 0 COLLISIONS.
Why it could not have found one: at stamp time the refs are genuinely EMPTY
ATTRSETS -- that emptiness is precisely why they fall to those branches. A
content signature computed there discriminates NOTHING, because there is no content
to sign. And separately, the one known 31-way collision DOES NOT PASS THROUGH THOSE
SITES AT ALL (0 stamp rows fleet-wide), so even a perfect content signature there
would have missed it. TWO independent reasons for a zero.

THE SIGHTED VERSION. Moved to the CONSUMPTION POINT -- collections.nix:205, where
`identity` and the GROUNDED content coexist -- and it immediately found:
    54 distinct keys, 84 distinct (key, content-name, stored-id) triples
    EXACTLY ONE key covering >1 content: 31 DISTINCT contents under one key
    the other 53: 1:1, all carrying a stored id_hash, all definition paths
★ The predicate found the 31-way collision IN THE SAME RUN in which it reported 53
clean keys. That is a positive control obtained for free from the measurement
itself -- the strongest available form, because the "clean" verdicts and the
"collision" verdict come from one instrument on one pass.

★ THE LAW THIS ADDS, and it is NOT the same as the earlier cases. The others failed
because the predicate could not MATCH (wrong pattern, dead control, unreachable
branch). This one failed because it looked at the RIGHT THING at the WRONG TIME.
A pipeline has stages, and a property about a RELATION between two values can only
be tested where BOTH VALUES EXIST. Here key exists at the mint and content exists
only after grounding; a check placed at the mint can never see the pair.
⇒ BEFORE TRUSTING ANY "no collision / no duplicate / all distinct" RESULT, ASK AT
WHICH STAGE EACH SIDE OF THE COMPARISON BECOMES AVAILABLE, AND CONFIRM THE
PREDICATE RUNS AT OR AFTER THE LATER ONE. A zero from before that point is not
evidence of absence; it is evidence the instrument was early.

COROLLARY EARNED IN THE SAME RUN: the author reported the blind version AS
discarded, with the reason. That is why the sighted result is trustworthy -- a
0-collisions verdict reported without the staging analysis would have looked
identical and been worthless.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
★ CASE ADDED 2026-07-28 -- A ONE-VARIABLE TEST ON A TWO-VARIABLE CAUSE READS AS A
REFUTATION. Self-falsified by the implementer, one round after it reported the
opposite conclusion to the orchestrator.

THE WRONG CONCLUSION, reported and recorded: "`__isPolicy` is wrong on those
fixtures -- they are on the KERNEL surface, where the plain record is correct."
That came from a run CONFOUNDED BY THE AUTHOR'S OWN `den.`-prefix corruption
(a blanket regex had silently moved `den.policies.self1` to `policies.self1`), and
it was tested by adding `__isPolicy` ALONE.

THE MEASURED TRUTH, three value shapes side by side in one run:
    bareFn / record / record + __isPolicy        -> NO src->dst edge   (all three identical)
    record + __isPolicy + selects = null         -> edge PRESENT
★ BOTH CONDITIONS ARE REQUIRED, AND NEITHER ALONE SHOWS ANYTHING:
  1. `__isPolicy = true` -- the v1 discriminator. Without it a kernel-shaped record
     on the compat surface is rejected LAZILY, so the rule silently never
     materialises.
  2. `selects = null` -- DECLARED. Without it the derivation correctly gives [ ],
     because the fixture registers the policy and includes it nowhere.
So adding `__isPolicy` alone produced no improvement, WHICH LOOKED LIKE EVIDENCE
THAT `__isPolicy` WAS THE WRONG HYPOTHESIS. It was necessary but not sufficient.

★ THE LAW: WHEN A CAUSE HAS TWO NECESSARY CONDITIONS, TESTING EITHER ONE ALONE
RETURNS THE SAME NULL RESULT AS TESTING A FALSE HYPOTHESIS. A single-variable
ablation cannot distinguish "this factor is irrelevant" from "this factor is one of
two". The null result is not evidence against the factor; it is evidence about the
EXPERIMENT'S ARITY.
⇒ Before concluding a factor is irrelevant from a no-change ablation, ask whether
anything ELSE must also hold for the effect to be observable -- and if the effect
is a PRESENCE (an edge, a firing, a materialised rule), enumerate everything that
gates that presence, because each gate independently suppresses the observation.
⇒ AND NOTE THE COMPOUNDING FAILURE: the wrong conclusion also rode a CONFOUNDED
TREE. Two defects in one measurement -- wrong arity and a corrupted baseline --
each sufficient to produce the same null.

COUNTER-EXAMPLE FROM THE SAME AGENT, SAME SESSION, showing the discipline working:
the `ambient` marking was ablated against THE WHOLE SUITE AND PARITY, and the
failure sets came back BYTE-IDENTICAL -- an honest inert verdict, with the ablation
scope wide enough that no second variable could hide in it. The difference is the
BREADTH of the ablation, not the intent of the ablator.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
★ CASE ADDED 2026-07-28 -- `tryEval(...).success` SWALLOWS THE ABORT, SO THE REAL
ERROR NEVER REACHES CI OUTPUT. A fixture idiom that converts a NAMED, ACTIONABLE
message into an anonymous boolean.

MEASURED: three compat-resolve failures presented in CI as bare value-mismatches
(actual false / expected true) with no diagnostic. The fixtures wrap the evaluation
in `tryEval(...).success`. Re-running the SAME fixture WITHOUT the tryEval produced
the cause verbatim on the first attempt:
    "den-hoag: policy registration: den.policies: `enroll` declares no `emits` -
     the declaration codomain is REQUIRED. `emits = [ ]` (produces nothing,
     compiles to no rule) is a legal value; an omitted `emits` is not, because
     silence must not be read as a permission to discover it by execution"
The migration's own new named guard, working exactly as designed -- and completely
invisible until the wrapper was removed.

★ THE LAW: A PREDICATE THAT COLLAPSES AN OUTCOME TO A BOOLEAN DISCARDS EVERY
DISTINCTION THE OUTCOME CARRIED. `tryEval(...).success == false` is true for the
abort you meant to pin, for a DIFFERENT abort, for a typo in the fixture, and for a
guard three migrations hence. It cannot tell them apart, and when it fails it tells
you nothing about why.
⇒ This is the same defect as `test-mixed-stratum-aborts`'s false pass earlier in
this arc -- there the boolean predicate went GREEN for the wrong reason; here it
goes RED with the reason erased. SAME INSTRUMENT, BOTH FAILURE DIRECTIONS.
⇒ REMEDY SHAPE: assert on the message TEXT, not on the boolean -- and pair it with a
NEGATIVE CONTROL in the same run showing the predicate discriminates on content
rather than on any abort occurring. That is the fix already applied to
b2-two-stratum and compat-policy-expansion in this same migration, so the pattern
exists in-tree; it simply has not been applied everywhere `tryEval` appears.

★ AND THE COROLLARY THAT MADE THIS FINDING CHEAP: when a failing test reports only
a boolean, THE FIRST MOVE IS TO REMOVE THE WRAPPER AND RE-RUN, before forming any
hypothesis about the cause. The diagnosis here took one run. Forming a hypothesis
first is what produced the 12-file corruption earlier the same evening.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
★ CASE ADDED 2026-07-28 -- THE AUDIT INSTRUMENT WAS THE AUDITED INSTRUMENT, ONE
LEVEL UP. The strongest form of predicate blindness yet recorded here, because no
better version of the predicate exists.

THE TASK: decide, for each policy whose codomain RECOVERS EMPTY at a fabricated
sentinel context, whether it is genuinely inert or a value-conditional body being
silently dropped.

THE INSTRUMENT SPECIFIED (by the orchestrator): re-fire each body against ALTERNATE
fabricated sentinels; differ ⇒ value-conditional; agree ⇒ inert.

THE SELF-REFUTATION, inside a single run: `vc-host` reported AGREES -- a policy
proven value-conditional by direct measurement minutes earlier. The three sentinel
variants carried class/system/hostName but no `settings`, and the body branches on
`host.settings.on or false`.

★★ THE LAW: AN INSTRUMENT THAT SHARES ITS SUBJECT'S DEFECT CANNOT AUDIT IT. The
census fabricates a context to ask whether fabricating a context was wrong. It
inherits the exact limitation under test, so it can only report "empty at the
contexts I happened to fabricate." POSITIVES ARE CONCLUSIVE, NEGATIVES ARE WORTHLESS
-- and no finite variant set repairs this, because the condition space is unbounded
(any field, any predicate).
⇒ THE DIAGNOSTIC QUESTION TO ASK OF ANY AUDIT: does my instrument make the same
assumption the thing under audit makes? If yes, its clean results are vacuous no
matter how many arms it has. MORE ARMS DO NOT FIX A SHARED PREMISE.
⇒ THE ESCAPE IS ALWAYS A DIFFERENT KIND OF EVIDENCE, not more of the same kind. Here:
the BODY'S SOURCE -- does it branch on a value? -- which is decidable by reading and
makes no fabricated context at all.

COMPARE, SAME SESSION, THE THREE OTHER SHAPES so the family is visible:
· predicate could not MATCH (wrong pattern / unreachable branch)
· predicate ran at the WRONG STAGE (both sides of the relation not yet in existence)
· predicate tested ONE variable of a TWO-variable cause (null reads as refutation)
· ★ and now: PREDICATE SHARES THE SUBJECT'S DEFECT (clean result is structurally
  vacuous; no version of this predicate can be sound)
The first three are fixable by a better predicate. THE FOURTH IS NOT.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
★★★ CASE ADDED 2026-07-28 -- A CORRUPTED TEST THAT WAS **GREEN**, AND THE ONLY
METHOD THAT COULD HAVE FOUND IT. This is the most important entry in this log,
because every other technique recorded here is FAILURE-DRIVEN and therefore
structurally blind to it.

WHAT HAPPENED. An oracle-driven migration script wrapped `poison` in a policy
record at two sites where `poison` is NOT a policy:
· ci/tests/no-fleet-flags.nix -- `poison` is a MODULE,
  `{ config, ... }: { config.den.aspects.boom = ...; }`  -> test went RED, found
· ★ ci/tests/compat-compile-golden.nix -- `poison` is a PARAMETRIC ASPECT BODY,
  `aspects.system.nixos = poison`  -> ★★ THE SUITE STAYED GREEN
The corruption turned a bare lambda into a record ON THE EXACT ROW whose comment
reads "the aspect row is near-identity passthrough, VALUES STAY THUNKS." So the
suite passed while testing something other than what it says it tests.

WHY THE SCRIPT DID IT. The oracle was HEAD's own MEASURED name->kind map -- sound
AS AN ORACLE. The script keyed on the NAME. Its `is_lambda` guard passed happily,
because A MODULE IS A LAMBDA and so is an aspect body.
★ THE LAW: A NAME-KEYED MAP CANNOT BE USED TO REWRITE NAME-KEYED SITES UNLESS THE
NAMESPACE IS THE SAME NAMESPACE. `poison` as a policy name and `poison` as a local
binding in a different fixture are different namespaces that happen to share
spellings. The oracle carried "what kind is the policy named X"; it could never
carry "every X in the tree is that policy."

★ FOURTH TURN OF ONE SCREW, and the author wrote the previous three down before
committing this one:
    a measured list is not a census
      -> a grep window is not a body boundary
        -> a module error is not a module cause
          -> ★ A NAME IS NOT A DEFINITION
Each proxy MORE credible than the last. A measured oracle is the most credible of
all, which is exactly why it was the one that did the most damage.

★★ AND THE METHOD THAT CAUGHT THE GREEN ONE, WHICH IS THE TRANSFERABLE PART:
A SIBLING SWEEP AFTER THE FIRST INSTANCE. The habit was recorded earlier the same
session after `homeDarwin-to-hm` was found sitting eleven lines below its declared
sibling. Applied here it immediately produced a SECOND instance -- one that WAS
PASSING and that NO FAILURE-DRIVEN METHOD WOULD EVER HAVE SURFACED.
⇒ EVERY OTHER INSTRUMENT IN THIS LOG READS FAILURES. Failure-set diffs, suite
counts, signature triage, root-cause chasing -- all of them start from something
being RED. A corrupted test that stays GREEN is invisible to all of them, and it is
strictly worse than a red one because it silently stops testing its subject.
⇒ THEREFORE: AFTER ANY MECHANICAL OR SCRIPTED EDIT, SWEEP FOR SIBLINGS OF EVERY
SITE TOUCHED -- INCLUDING IN FILES THAT STAYED GREEN. "Zero newly failing" does not
mean "nothing else was changed"; it means "nothing else was changed IN A WAY A TEST
NOTICED." Those are different claims and only one of them is what the diff shows.
(This is the sharper form of the earlier entry "zero newly failing is not zero newly
weakened" -- there the weakening was in tests already red; here it is in a test that
is green and stayed green.)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
★ TWO CASES ADDED 2026-07-29, BOTH SELF-REPORTED, AND THE FIRST COMPLETES A PAIR.

★★ CASE 1 -- THE MIRROR: AN ERROR I DID READ IS NOT FAILURE.
A `git push` reported:
    ! [remote rejected] main -> main (cannot lock ref 'refs/heads/main':
      is at d775ea80... but expected 5f38b961...)
    error: failed to push some refs
AND IT HAD SUCCEEDED. A ref-lock race: the ref had already advanced to that very commit
when the lock was taken. `git fetch` then showed origin/main == d775ea8, no ahead/behind,
and `git cat-file -e origin/main:<spec>` confirmed the file on the remote.
★ PAIRED WITH THE CASE RECORDED HOURS EARLIER THE SAME SESSION: a `git commit` returned
with no error I read AND HAD NOT COMMITTED (pre-commit refused; HEAD stayed put), caught
only because the author printed the SHA immediately after.
⇒ ★★ THE COMPLETE RULE, BOTH DIRECTIONS: AN ERROR YOU DID NOT READ IS NOT SUCCESS, AND AN
ERROR YOU DID READ IS NOT FAILURE. NEITHER THE EXIT PATH NOR THE ABSENCE OF A COMPLAINT IS
THE EVIDENCE. CHECK THE STATE -- the SHA, the ref, the object on the remote.
★ POSTSCRIPT ON THE CAUSE, recorded because "mysterious race" was the wrong diagnosis: THE
RACE WAS THE ORCHESTRATOR. I told the author to push, it went idle without reporting, I
verified the commit myself and pushed it, and its push then found the ref already advanced.
A git anomaly with a coordination cause. ⇒ WHEN TWO ACTORS CAN WRITE THE SAME REF, "who
pushed" is part of the state and must be asked before an anomaly is diagnosed as one.

★★ CASE 2 -- A DEPENDENCY RECORDED IN ONE FILE IS NOT A DEPENDENCY UNDERSTOOD.
The author was ruled, on the retargeted exclude-family witness, that the retirement of
`excludeFamilyUntagged` DEPENDS on a declared codomain, and WROTE THAT DEPENDENCY INTO
`compat-exclude-family.nix`'s COMMENT. It then authored a design whose central move CREATES
A CLASS OF POLICIES WITH NO CODOMAIN -- breaking the precondition it had just recorded --
and did not carry the dependency across. It found this AFTER freezing, and messaged rather
than edited.
★ Its own words: "A DEPENDENCY RECORDED IN ONE FILE IS NOT A DEPENDENCY I HAVE UNDERSTOOD."
⇒ THE LESSON IS ABOUT WHERE OBLIGATIONS LIVE. Writing a precondition into the comment at the
site that satisfies it does NOT put it in front of the person who later violates it
elsewhere. The graph is where a cross-cutting obligation survives; a comment is where it is
findable only by someone already standing in the right file.
⇒ PRACTICALLY: when a retirement or simplification is justified BY a precondition, file the
precondition as a bead edge against the construct it constrains -- not only as a comment at
the construct that currently satisfies it. This is the third time this arc that a retiring
construct turned out to be discharging an obligation nobody had written where it would be
seen (cf. the staged pre-pass and ABW condition 2).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
★★ CASE ADDED 2026-07-29 -- AN ASYMPTOTIC ARGUMENT NAMES A GROWTH RATE, NOT A VARIABLE.
The clearest vindication in the arc of spec-before-development covering one-line gen-lib
changes, and it came from measuring three "obvious" fixes before applying any of them.

An independent audit filed three quadratic-primitive findings, all ARGUED from source, and
sequenced them as "highest multiplier per line changed -- do these early regardless of the
rest. Three small library edits, every consumer benefits, no den-hoag change required."
MEASURED WITH OPERATION COUNTS (NIX_SHOW_STATS on a plain file, which sidesteps a 345 ms
flake floor that had defeated an earlier timing attempt; a linear-dedup positive control
showed exactly 2x per doubling, so the instrument can distinguish linear from quadratic):

· ONE CONFIRMED AND WORTH DOING (`groupBy`: 4x per doubling vs 0 for the builtin).
· ONE CONFIRMED WITH ITS SCALE CLAIM ~3x HIGH IN TWO INDEPENDENT WAYS (`firstSeenBy`: the
  cost is N(N-1)/2+N not N^2, AND the corpus is 70 cells not 200 -- so 36x, not 100x).
· ★★ ONE REFUTED, WITH ITS NAMED FIX MEASURING **272x WORSE** THAN THE DEFECT.

THE REFUTED ONE IS THE LESSON. `unique` is quadratic; `dedupByKey` sits 75 lines above with
O(1) membership; the swap looks free. But `dedupByKey`'s recursion calls `builtins.tail`,
WHICH COPIES -- so it is quadratic IN LIST LENGTH, while `unique` is quadratic IN DISTINCT
COUNT. ★ THE TWO ARE QUADRATIC IN DIFFERENT VARIABLES. At den-hoag's real input shape (11,418
calls, median N=1, max N=24, 7.8% with N>1) the "slow" one costs 1,179 and the "fast" one
320,779.
★ THE READING ERROR IS EXACT AND REPEATABLE: the finding read "O(1) membership" and stopped.
It never asked WHICH VARIABLE each implementation is quadratic in, because both were labelled
by their membership test rather than by their copying.

⇒ THE LAW: AN ASYMPTOTIC ARGUMENT ESTABLISHES A GROWTH RATE. IT DOES NOT ESTABLISH THE
VARIABLE, AND IT SAYS NOTHING ABOUT THE INPUT SHAPE A PARTICULAR CONSUMER ACTUALLY PASSES.
Before swapping a primitive on complexity grounds, measure BOTH the consumer's real input
distribution AND the candidate's cost in the SAME variable. "The linear algorithm is right
there" was true about the asymptotic class and false about this consumer.
⇒ AND IT VINDICATES THE STANDING RULE CONCRETELY: two of three one-line changes would have
been wrong -- one an outright regression, one shipped with a cost claim 3x its real size --
and both were "proven" by a source reading that was correct as far as it went.
★ NOTE ALSO: the same remedy (`dedupByKey`) is RIGHT for one bead and a 272x REGRESSION for
another. A remedy is not transferable between findings that share a symptom.

NEW CASE — LAW 3 (a SOUND predicate proving a DIFFERENT proposition), SELF-INFLICTED BY THE ORCHESTRATOR, 2026-07-28.

MEASUREMENT, correct: .beads/beads.jsonl has 94 rows, all _type "issue", ZERO comment rows (Counter over the file). Comments exist and are load-bearing — bd show renders the owner comment resetting the exit condition.
PROPOSITION REPORTED, wrong: 'the durable record is lossy, so any audit reading it produces a false-clean.' Filed as P1 with two dependency edges onto real work.
OWNER: 'the beads .jsonl file isnt the source of truth, its an export for the beads viewer utility for me to inspect the current state.'

★ WHAT MAKES THIS THE SHARPEST INSTANCE YET: the refuting evidence was IN MY HAND AND QUOTED IN THE BEAD BODY. CLAUDE.md says '.beads/issues.jsonl is a passive export'; I cited that sentence while filing under the opposite framing. So this was not a missing check — it was a check performed, recorded, and not read against the conclusion.

⇒ REINFORCES, and sharpens, law 3: after a clean run, restate the conclusion and ask which command bears on THAT SENTENCE — and specifically re-read the evidence you already wrote down. A correct measurement adjacent to a wrong proposition is the hardest error to catch, because the citation looks like support.
⇒ SECOND-ORDER COST, the reason this is worth a case rather than a note: the wrong framing PROPAGATED into a dispatch prompt, which told an agent the jsonl was the durable record. The agent noticed and said so. Wrong premises in briefs get inherited unless the brief invites refutation.

comments.author: Jason Bowman
comments.text:
NEW CASE — AN IDLE NOTIFICATION IS NOT EVIDENCE OF COMPLETION, AND THE ESTABLISHED RULE COVERED ONLY ONE DIRECTION. 2026-07-28.

STANDING RULE, earned earlier in this arc: agents report by MESSAGE, plain-text output is invisible, and SIX apparent silences were agents that had finished the work and written a report nobody could see ⇒ 'ping once, do not re-dispatch, check the scratchpad, the work is usually done.'
TODAY, THE INVERSE: an agent applied round 1 of a doc-correction task, reported it in full, then went idle having SILENTLY NOT APPLIED ROUND 2 — the follow-up instruction seemingly arriving as it finished. From the notification alone the two cases are IDENTICAL: 'idle, no report'.

MEASURED, which is the whole point: md5 of both target files was UNCHANGED from the round-1 result; the strings round 2 was meant to remove ('28×' at two sites, a stale verbatim quote, a wrong binding name) were all still present. One command settled it.

⇒ THE RULE AS WRITTEN INVITED THE WRONG INFERENCE. 'The work is usually done' is a prior, not a measurement, and it fails in the direction that looks like success. Corrected standing form: AN IDLE IS NOT EVIDENCE EITHER WAY — MEASURE THE ARTEFACT. `md5sum` + line count + a grep for the specific string the round should have changed. Then ping, with the measurement quoted, so the agent is not asked to re-derive what you already know.

★ FAMILY: this is the same shape as the rest of this log — a signal that CANNOT DISTINGUISH two states being read as though it distinguishes them. A grep that cannot match, a probe that cannot fire, a control that forces only a spine, and now a notification that carries no information about the artefact. In every case the fix is identical: go and look at the thing itself.

comments.text:
★ NEW TRAP — A COST COMPARISON WHOSE WORKLOAD CONTAINS THE GUARD'S OWN FIXTURES MEASURES THE FIXTURE, NOT THE GUARD. And it fails in the flattering direction. 2026-07-28.

MEASURED: the first cost run for the supportedness law had the new test file staged in BOTH trees and reported the law CHEAPER — nrThunks −204,688 (−0.1384%), nrFunctionCalls −196,749 (−0.1805%). A guard that adds work appeared to remove it.
CAUSE: on the PATCHED tree the four abort fixtures SHORT-CIRCUIT, and one of them (`test-negative-cycle-aborts-at-the-crossing`) stops building an entire `nixosConfiguration`. The work the guard SAVES BY ABORTING swamped the work it COSTS. Both trees ran 'the same tests' and that was exactly the problem.
CORRECTED: exclude the guard's own fixtures from both sides. Clean result — +0.4762% thunks, +0.4110% calls, reproducing the spec's independently-derived figures.

⇒ GENERAL FORM, and it is not limited to guards: WHEN THE THING YOU ARE MEASURING CHANGES WHETHER PART OF THE WORKLOAD RUNS AT ALL, THE WORKLOAD IS NOT A CONSTANT AND THE DIFFERENCE IS NOT THE COST. Anything that aborts, short-circuits, caches, or prunes has this shape. The test to apply before quoting a delta: DOES THE PATCHED TREE DO THE SAME WORK, OR MERELY RUN THE SAME COMMAND?
★ AND NOTE THE DIRECTION — it made a real cost look like a saving. A trap that flatters the change is far more dangerous than one that penalises it, because nobody re-measures a pleasant result. This joins the standing list beside 'a sound predicate proving a different proposition': the command was correct, the trees were correct, the comparison was not.

SELF-CAUGHT by the implementing agent, which noticed that a guard adding a check could not plausibly reduce total work and went looking rather than reporting the number.
